title: He Taught Helen Frankenthaler to Paint. In 1951 She Showed Her Old Teacher What Painting Had Become.
standfirst: Paul Feeley had chaired Bennington College's art department for over a decade, drilling students in realist technique, when a former student came back and introduced him to the painting her own generation was making. What he built over the next three years left behind a catalogue named for Roman generals and fixed stars. This undated canvas carries none of those names at all.

sections.heading: The Picture That Reset His Career Was One Red Shape, Placed and Left Alone
sections.body: In 1954 Feeley made a canvas he later treated as the hinge of his whole career: a single red form on a green ground, [oil and enamel on canvas](https://archive.studiointernational.com/SI1968/july-august/files/basic-html/page47.html), 65 by 42 inches, credited today to his estate by way of New York's Betty Parsons Gallery. He called it Red Blotch, and described the shift it marked in blunt terms of his own: all the time he had spent, he said, "breaking up space in exciting and dynamic ways turned me toward a conception of movement which was almost the contradiction of what you might call the dynamic and the exciting." What replaced it was not an accumulation of brush decisions but close to the opposite of one: "I just sensed the shape of the canvas as an event, as against the notion of the canvas creating an arena for events." Abstract (Red and Yellow) carries no year in the record and no title beyond a description of its own colours — worth pausing on, given how exactly, and how differently, Feeley usually named things.

sections.heading: He Learned to Draw Again on Kleenex and Clorox
sections.body: Between 1943 and 1946 Feeley left teaching to serve with the Marines in the Pacific; his own estate's chronology states that he was among the first Marines into Nagasaki after the bombing. There was no painting to be done in that stretch of his life. The critic Gene Baro, writing Feeley's memorial essay for Studio International in 1968, recorded what filled the gap instead: "during his war years, Feeley had no opportunity to paint. He took to drawing, wherever and whenever materials came to hand" — "he drew on scraps of paper, on pages of books, even on odd pieces of Kleenex. Drawings of his survive made with clorox washes." Baro reads the habit as more than improvisation: it was, he wrote, "in the duress of war and in the boredom of camp life" that Feeley "came back to the emotion and directness of drawing." The same instinct to pare a mark down to exactly what it needed, no more material and no more gesture than the moment required, is the discipline that resurfaces, a decade later, in Red Blotch.

sections.heading: The Student Who Taught the Teacher
sections.body: Feeley had taught at Bennington College since 1939 and chaired its art department through the 1950s, drilling undergraduates in a realist technique descended from his own training under Thomas Hart Benton and Cecilia Beaux at the Art Students League. One of those undergraduates, Helen Frankenthaler, left Bennington for New York's contemporary scene, and in the spring of 1951, by Baro's account, came back and introduced her former teacher to it — alongside the critic Clement Greenberg. Feeley was over forty by then: more than a decade into teaching life drawing to eighteen-year-olds, being shown by a recent student what painters barely older than her were doing with a canvas. Red Blotch did not follow for another two to three years, and nothing about it looks like a Frankenthaler stain painting. Whatever he took from that introduction, he spent the rest of the decade turning into something that resembled no one else's version of it.

sections.heading: He Staged Pollock's Bennington Retrospective and Painted Nothing Like Him
sections.body: Through the 1950s Feeley used his position at Bennington to put on exhibitions for exactly the kind of painting his own work was moving away from: a David Smith retrospective in 1951, a Jackson Pollock retrospective in 1952, Hans Hofmann in 1955, and a Kenneth Noland show in 1961, each organised with Clement Greenberg. For a few years a small college in rural Vermont hung Pollock and Smith's work alongside a faculty whose own painting had deliberately turned its back on gestural abstraction. Baro's 1968 essay records Feeley's own account of why: expressionism's stress on accident and incident had become, in his word, "unbearable" — its "heart-on-the-sleeve effect" pushing him toward "decorum" instead. He went on curating the painters who worked the other way without ever painting like them again.

sections.heading: By 1964 Every Canvas Had a Name From the Sky. This One Still Doesn't Have a Date.
sections.body: Feeley's own titles, [listed in sequence](https://www.wikiart.org/en/paul-feeley/all-works/text-list), tell a story this picture sits outside of: a run of ancient Mediterranean place names in the late 1950s and early 1960s — Tenos, Ios, Thera, Minoa, Carthage, Sybaris — then Roman names — Cassius, Trajan, Germanicus, Remus — and then, from 1964 on, a run of works named for stars pulled from an astronomical catalogue rather than from anything visible in the paint: Alioth, Alruccabah, Etamin, Gomelza, Denib El Delphini. Against that run, Abstract (Red and Yellow) is the plain exception — the only descriptively titled, undated work in WikiArt's listing of Feeley's paintings, filed alongside three other canvases simply called Untitled. One of those three, Cheleb, actually carries a firm 1965 date in the catalogue behind Feeley's own 1968 Guggenheim memorial — a reminder that "undated" in one database is a gap in that database, not necessarily a fact about the painting. Feeley did not live to be asked which was true of this one. He died on 10 June 1966, seven weeks short of his fifty-sixth birthday, of leukemia, at Memorial Hospital in New York — twelve years into the run that had started with Red Blotch. The Guggenheim's memorial retrospective followed two years later; a fuller reckoning, Imperfections by Chance, did not reach a museum again until the Albright-Knox took it on in November 2014, forty-eight years after his death.
